At the time of its construction, the bridge was a significant connector between
Washington and Idaho that ran along a major interstate highway between the
states. It was known to be an innovative design that featured the use of a unique
mechanical-electrical lift system utilizing cables and counterweights. The bridge
is an excellent example of a lift span bridge that utilizes an innovative lift design
called “synchro-tie,” it is one of the earliest and last remaining examples of this in
Idaho and Washington.

concrete reinforcing, earthen fill, two 136-ft. concrete half-wall railings,
and approaches, arches, and single instream bent. Signs of its board
form construction are visible along the interior of each arch barrel.

Daniel B. Luten. Constructed in 1920, the structure is one of two confirmed “Luten
Arches” in Chelan County, both built in the early 1920s by the same company.
Genuine Luten designed arch bridges are increasingly rare in the state as few
patented Luten Arches remain on Washington roads. Repairs to its handrail
performed with dissimilar concrete detract from its integrity of materials and
feeling. However, the bridge retains the majority of its integrity of location,
workmanship, design, and setting.

The structure is a 250-foot long riveted and pin-connected steel
Pennsylvania Petit through truss. The bridge retains integrity of
workmanship and design as evidenced by its ornate portal braces that
resemble a waffle pattern set askew. Curved L-shaped pieces set below
the portal brace frame the bridge entrance.

Berry; Builders Bowerman and
McCloy, American Bridge Company

Constructed in 1908 by Chelan County, the bridge carried traffic over the Entiat
River until it was removed from vehicle service. It is likely the bridge played a
minor role in the transportation and settlement of Chelan County and the Entiat
River Valley as the introduction of rail already established and increased
settlement and commerce in the area in the early 1890s.

Pin-connection Pratt through truss, dual span construction. The two steel
through truss spans erected in the Pratt configuration are the primary
character-defining features of the bridge.

Chelan County constructed the bridge in 1909 and reportedly “rebuilt” it in 1927.
The County converted the bridge to sole pedestrian use in the early 1990s. The
bridge is a rare surviving example of a dual span pin-connected Pratt through truss
built in the early twentieth century.

The structure is a 641.0-foot long cantilever deck truss. The bridge retains
integrity of design as evidenced by historic steel railings and truss
configuration.

Bridges have spanned the Wenatchee river in this location since 1892, before that
a cable ferry was used to move people and goods across the river. Three bridges
were built prior to the Wenatchee Avenue Northbound Bridge. In 1955 the
Southbound bridge was built to alleviate the high traffic on the 1933 bridge.

Its design represents an era when post-tensioning was in its

design and construction as illustrated in its 70 ft. concrete girder and
concrete spiral ramps. This bridge is a good example of one of the first

Completed in 1965, the bridge was one of the first post-tensioned, pre-stressed,

among the first to employ high strength concrete to accommodate the post-
tensioning process. It utilizes special engineering and technical skill in its design
as illustrated by its main girder and spiral ramps.

This is a three span, reinforced concrete flat slab bridge having span
lengths of 50, 101 and 50 feet. The supports at Piers 2 and 3 consist of
four inclined frame legs that taper in width in the longitudinal direction
from 2-feet at the bottom to 4-feet at the top and then blend in smoothly
with the soffit of the slab.

The use of the inclined legs is an early example of utilizing a different structural
configuration to accommodate the locations of the foundations for crossing the
ravine and minimize the construction costs. The bridge appears to be an
important route for the local traffic to cross the deep ravine. The structure has a
pleasing, smooth and an attractive appearance.

project, highlighting the relationship between the Reynolds Aluminum
factory and the community.

the manmade Lake Sacajawea. All structural components were to be made out of
aluminum unless otherwise necessary.

is located on the Old Pacific Highway. In 1953 the 4-lane US Highway 99 was
routed to the bridge creating the need to re-striped the bridge for 4-lanes. This
design lasted until 1969 when the twin bridges were built over the Toutle river west

With a total length of 1,208 feet, the George Sellar Bridge is one of the
state’s most impressive crossings of the Columbia River. The structure’s
most distinctive feature is its steel tied arch, which rises 180 feet above
low water level. The deck trusses are Warren-type configurations with
vertical bracing. Oval openings in the portal braces add esthetic appeal
to the bridge deck while reducing steel weight and cost.

In its Twenty-second Biennial Report for 1946-48, the Department of Highways
described the George Sellar Bridge as the most important structure of the 73
bridges being built at the time. It was then a vital link on Primary State Highway 2,
the northernmost cross-state route prior to completion of the North Cascades
Highway 20. It appears that the use of cantilevered steel spans with a suspended
thru tied arch was the first such design on the state’s highway system. In 1951 the
American Institute of Steel Construction bestowed on the Sellar Bridge its Class I
Award for the most beautiful bridge comprising one or more spans over 400 feet
built in the U.S. in 1950.

Approximately 300 tons of structural carbon and silicon steel were used.

In late 1934, the Bureau of Reclamation began the construction of a 950 foot
through cantilever steel truss across the Columbia River near the site of the Grand
Coulee Dam. The bridge was designed by the Washington Department of
Highways for the Columbia Basin Commission to serve a dual purpose. It would
be used to transport heavy equipment across the Columbia during the
construction of the dam, and after the dam's completion, it would be used as a
permanent highway structure on State Route 155.

1,831 ft. across the Snake River on a northwest-southeast orientation. It
carries two lanes of State Route 285 and connects Whitman and Garfield
counties. Both steel tied arch trusses are comprised of sixteen panels
measuring 32 ft.-6 in each with two abutting Warren through trusses
composed of eight panels with the same dimensions.

configuration built in Washington. The other two are the Pioneer Memorial “Blue”
Bridge (395/40), completed in 1954, and the Columbia River Bridge at Beebe
(12/420), built in 1962. It retains a high degree of integrity as no significant
alterations have occurred to the structure since its completion. Originally a
segment of Primary State Highway No. 3, also known as the Inland Empire
Highway, the highway was designated State Route 127 in 1970.

The Black River Bridge (12/76) is a 169 ft. riveted steel Warren pony truss
with vertical members and a polygonal top chord. The 169 ft. long bridge
is comprised of a 104 ft. main span with trusses of six 17 ft. 4 in. panels
and two 32 ft. long concrete T-beam approach spans with hunched
girders. Concrete balustrade railings extend along the sides of the
approaches from the ends of the trusses.

Washington State Department of

The Black River Bridge a Warren pony truss, an increasingly rare bridge type in
Washington State. The structure possesses a polygonal top chord, a subtype of
the more common Warren pony with a parallel top chord. The Black River Bridge
was built in 1932 on a spur of what was then State Road No. 9, called the Olympic
Highway, that encircled the Olympic Peninsula. In 1970 the highway crossing the
bridge became U.S. 12.

The Hoquiam River Bridge (101/125E), completed in 1971, is a steel truss
vertical lift bridge spanning the Hoquiam River on US 101 in Hoquiam.
The bridge’s total length is 464.9 feet. The central lift span is 233.9 feet
long, the deck width is 27.9 feet, and the vertical clearance above deck is
17.7 feet.

Department of Highways, W. T.
Robinson, Willis B. Horn, Carl M.
West, George Stevens

The bridge project was part of the “Aberdeen-Hoquiam one-way couplet,”
designed to relieve traffic congestion caused by motorists heading west to the
ocean. The new route carried US Route 101’s eastbound traffic from the couplet in
Aberdeen to Riverside Avenue and 16th Street in Hoquiam.

The City of Hoquiam, with assistance from the State, funded the
construction of a double leaf Strauss trunnion bascule bridge over the
Hoquiam River in 1928. The 1980 foot structure consists of a 200 foot
bascule span, one 120 foot steel Pratt truss, one 150 foot Pratt steel
truss, and concrete girder and timber trestle approach spans.

The City of Hoquiam, with assistance from the State, funded the construction of a
double leaf Strauss trunnion bascule bridge over the Hoquiam River in 1928. The
Hoquiam River Bridge is the only Strauss patented double-leaf bascule bridge
built before 1940 within the State. J.B. Strauss was a prolific bridge designer, and
was one of the early innovators in modern bascule bridge design. The distinctive
feature of the Strauss trunnion bascule is the pivoting of the counterweight which
moves parallel to itself at all times.

The Wishkah River Bridge is a classic, intact example of a riveted steel,
single-leaf (span), heel-trunnion bascule bridge. The bridge is 363 ft long
and 37 ft wide, with a 27 ft wide road deck and 5 ft wide sidewalks along
either side. The sidewalks have metal lattice handrails along their outer
edge, while modern-period tubular steel railings run between the
sidewalks and the road deck. The bascule span is a 145 ft Warren
through-truss with lateral overhead bracing and inclined end posts.

In 1924 the City of Aberdeen commissioned the construction of Wishkah River
Bridge. This is a classic example of the Strauss "heel-trunnion" bascule bridge. The
bridge carries westbound traffic of U.S. Route 12 across the Wishkah River. This
steel draw bridge connects Aberdeen with East Aberdeen. Its construction
lessened the need for ferries across the Wishkah, and improved automobile
access to the north shore of the harbor. The Bridge has all of the glamour of a
dockside crane. This is appropriate, for the bridge built in a busy, hard-working,
pragmatic harbor town.

The Heron Street Bridge retains considerable historical integrity. Its
essential historic character is preserved in the plate-girder swing span,
the concrete center pivot, and its hydraulic operating system. The Heron
Street Bridge consists of two riveted plate-girder spans: a single, 45 ft-
long approach span with a concrete deck connects the west-side bridge
seat with a 187 ft-long swing span.

The Heron Street Bridge crosses the Wishkah River in Aberdeen. It was considered
significant by the consulting engineers because of its “unusual” hydraulic system,
which raises and swings the center span to allow boat passage on the Wishkah
River. It is one of five historic-era swing bridges in Washington, and the only one
that is not a steel through-truss. In 1944, the state highway system included 16
swing bridges; only two of those bridges have survived.

Washington. Completed in 1965, the structure parallels an identical bridge
(12/51S) on State Route 12. In 1967, both bridges were selected by the American
Institute of Steel Construction as “The Most Beautiful Short Span Bridge” built in
the United States that year.

The Satsop River Bridge (12/51S) is a 410 ft. long bridge with a 279 ft.
riveted steel tied arch main span, flanked by one 65 ft. pre-stressed

adjacent north. The Satsop Bridge possesses artistically design elements that set
it apart from others of the same type. The structure is a rare type in Washington as
few have been erected on the state highway system.

The Chehalis River Bridge crosses seasonal wetlands and one of the
region’s major rivers that is subject to more than occasional flooding. The
bridge’s 37 timber trestle spans and one concrete box girder span cross
wetlands of the Chehalis River, while four concrete box girder spans
serve as the north approaches.

The Chehalis River Bridge’s main span (300 feet) is among the four longest in
Washington. Although its portal braces have been damaged and other structural
problems have warranted posting of load restrictions, the bridge’s primary
character-defining feature, the Warren truss, is essentially intact.

The Panhandle Bridge is a 185 foot steel plate girder vertical lift bridge.
The east approach has a 125 foot concrete deck slab and was replaced
in 1973, the west approach is a 95 foot untreated timber trestle was
reconstructed in 1974.

The Panhandle bridge goes over the East Fork of the Hoquaim River. The Hoquiam
River’s name comes from a Native American word meaning “hungry for wood”
describing the mountains of driftwood that accumulate at the river’s mouth. This
region was known for lumber production.

The Panhandle Bridge is a 1080 foot bridge with a 200 foot deck truss and

The bridge is located near Oakville, WA, a small town that historically has been

Money Creek Bridge is a 220 foot long continuous concrete box girder
bridge. The roadway is 14 ft wide with 2.5 ft sidewalks and carries two
lanes of traffic.

Money Creek Bridge is part of the Old Cascade Scenic Highway Heritage Corridor.
Construction of a serviceable road over Stevens Pass came relatively late to King
County due to the elevation and rugged terrain. Locals formed a Good Roads Club
to promote a cross-Cascades highway in 1912. Road construction was delayed by
WWI, it wasn't until 1925 that the road was open to automobiles. Money Creek
Bridge is the Eastern end of the Heritage Corridor.

Evens Creek Bridge is a 33 foot long continuous concrete girder bridge.
The roadway is brick masonry, 24 ft wide, and carries two lanes. The
bridge is low profile and barely distinguishable from the roadway. There
are modern guardrails on both sides of the bridge.

The historic Evens Creek bridge still has it's original brick roadway and is a rural
road a mile north of the SR-202 Cascade Valley Heritage Corridor. North Bend has
been a gateway between the Puget Sound and the Cascade Mountains for
hundreds of years.

52 ft wide and carries two lanes of traffic. The cast concrete railing with

trees and goes over Gardiners Creek.

The unique bridge serves as an aqueduct caring sew over Lake
Washington Blvd. The 180 ft structure consisting of six 30 ft arches. The
concrete surfacing was disguised with ornamental brick facing imitating
the rough texture, and assuming the grandeur of many of the old masonry
arches. The walkway is narrow, two people can walk abreast. The bridge
has masonry railing and distinctive historic globe lamps.

In 1910, Mr. R.H. Thomson, Seattle City Engineer, contracted the building of a
reinforced concrete arch viaduct to carry a newly constructed sewer line across
low ground in Washington Park. One individual observed in a letter to the City
Engineering Department in 1912: "The bridge is not an 'appurtenance of the sewer.
It is a piece of ornamental bridge architecture designed elaborately and is a very
much greater thing than the sewer itself, in every way." The bridge was designed by
the newly formed architectural firm of Wilcox and Sayward.

Concrete bridge with a distinctive cast concrete trefoil railing running the
length of the roadway. Ornamental stone is above the arch. The bridge is
located in Frink Park which was designed by the Olmsted Brothers. From
the bridge a manmade waterfall designed by the Olmsted's can be seen.

The Olmsted brothers actively worked to have the ravine that is now Frink Park
designated as a park, claiming that it would not be suitable for housing
development. The land was donated by J.M. Frink in 1906. The Olmstead brothers
laid out the curving alignment for Lake Washington Blvd, designed a trail system
through the park, and added focal points with benches and pools. The bridge has
become a main attraction for park visitors.

The Daily Olympian called the bridge "Washington's first venture in ornamental
construction and the latest link in the rapidly advancing state highway system…"
The newspaper goes on to say that the special artistic effort of the totem pole
pylons, sixteen sodium vapor lights, precast railings, and other embellishments
"was attributable to the fact it is the approach to the capital city." While a
beautiful entrance to the capital city was wanted, the bridge was part of a safer,
direct approach through Tumwater to Olympia which eliminated one of the Pacific
Highway's most hazardous sections containing five right-angle turns.

spans 14.5 miles intersects with the 22-mile Chehalis Western Trail.

The Julia Butler Hansen Bridge is the only bridge crossing a channel, but not the
entire width, of the Columbia River, it ending the isolation of residents of Puget
Island, the largest island in the river, and providing access to the ferry connecting
the island and Oregon. It has an intact steel Warren through truss, erected by the
cantilever method, and Warren deck truss. Although its original timber trusses and
trestle south approach spans were replaced with concrete and steel girders in the
1980s, the essential character-defining features of the bridge, its Warren deck
truss and cantilevered Warren trusses and lattice steel handrails are intact and
convey a sense of the structure’s historic character.

This is a one-lane covered bridge with vertical board siding. The support
is mainly pilings and timbers. The roof has a small arch. In 1905, a two-
span timber Howe truss was constructed across Grays River. The trusses
were covered and reinforced with cables in 1908 in order to protect the
structural members from exposure to the elements, thus increasing the
longevity of the timber components.

In 1905, a two-span timber Howe truss was constructed across Grays River at a
cost of $2,700 to facilitate access to State Route 830 for dairy farmers living in the
vicinity. Although the covered bridge was once a common means of extending the
short life span of timber structures, there are only four covered bridges remaining
in Washington. The Grays River Bridge is the oldest of the covered bridges in the
State, and the only one that remains part of a public highway.

This bridge, originally called First Street Bridge No. 335, was built in 1918 within
the Town of Farmington, apparently a municipal project. Today the bridge remains
in use, owned and maintained by the Town of Farmington. Although engineering
plans were not located, the bridge appears to be a Daniel B. Luten reinforced
concrete filled spandrel deck arch design, a typical example of Luten’s highway
bridge structures. The bridge plaque identifies the builder as H. C. Malott, a
Seattle bridge contractor.

Both trusses are in the Warren configuration, denoted by the standard

the standard Warren design as evidenced by its parabolic top chord
which is comprised of five steel I-beam sections connected via riveted
plates and built-up vertical members set between each diagonal
members.

The bridge is the second oldest pony truss bridge in use in Washington State. Its
timber decking was replaced in-kind in 2007 as part of its conversion to

constructed on Zillah Heights Road the same year. The structure was needed to
span the canal to provide readable access to nearby fruit orchards.
